# Telephone (`telephone`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electromagnetism; helped by electric_battery, electric_telegraph, wave_nature_light_sound, ohms_law_circuits
- Core idea: Sound is a rapid to-and-fro of air pressure. In the transmitter a thin diaphragm presses on loosely packed carbon grains through which a battery current flows; pressure changes the resistance of the carbon, so the current copies the sound wave. In the receiver this varying current passes through a coil on a small permanent magnet and pulls a thin iron diaphragm to and fro, which reproduces the sound. Two wires twisted together for each line keep out noise from neighbouring lines, and an exchange with a switchboard connects any two subscribers. The band from about 300 to 3,400 vibrations per second is enough for clear speech.
- Pitfalls:
  - Sending speech as on/off currents like a telegraph; the current must vary smoothly in step with the sound
  - Leaving the permanent magnet out of the receiver: the diaphragm then moves at twice the frequency and the speech is garbled
  - Using Bell's first magneto transmitter for long lines; it is far too weak, the carbon transmitter with a battery is what made the telephone practical
  - Using single wires with earth return side by side; subscribers hear each other and every telegraph nearby
  - Presenting the priority as simple: Reis, Meucci, Gray and Bell all have claims and the patent history is still argued over
- History: europe: 1861 – Philipp Reis's 'Telephon' transmits tones and some speech (Frankfurt); 1878 Hughes's carbon microphone; americas: 1871 – Meucci's caveat in New York (its content is disputed); February–March 1876 – Bell's patent, filed the same day as Gray's caveat, and first transmitted sentence; 1877–1878 carbon transmitters (Edison, Berliner); 1878 first commercial exchange, New Haven; 1891 Strowger's automatic exchange; 1915 New York–San Francisco line with vacuum-tube repeaters
- Read:
  - Robert V. Bruce, Bell: Alexander Graham Bell and the Conquest of Solitude (1973)
  - Claude S. Fischer, America Calling: A Social History of the Telephone to 1940 (1992)
